newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FOCUS-IMF,WBank seek action on Albania investment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-IMF,WBank seek action on Albania investment.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund and World Bank have urged Albanian authorities, with a week to go in an election campaign, to act quickly to regulate investment schemes after collapses triggered mass unrest.
A letter sent by the heads of the IMF and World Bank at the weekend asked President Sali Berisha to enact as quickly as possible a decree on controlling such schemes.
"Action on this is a precondition for a successful recovery," IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus and World Bank President James Wolfensohn said in the letter faxed to Reuters on Monday.
"In this regard, the draft presidential decree just approved by the Council of Ministers is most welcome and we strongly urge you to sign it into law as soon as possible."

Both lenders, it said, were prepared to provide assistance "once Albanian authorities are in control of the country...and have made progress in establishing a sound macroeconomic framework and dealing effectively with the schemes".
The IMF has disbursed about $60 million in credits to Albania since 1992, but loans were suspended in 1995. The World Bank has provided nearly $300 million in credits.

Progress in enacting the legislation has been slowed by a row pitting Berisha against Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, a member of the Socialist Party challenging the president's Democratic Party in next Sunday's legislative election.

Five "pyramid" schemes, in which interest to old depositors is paid with deposits from new investors, collapsed earlier this year, swallowing up the life savings of hundreds of thousands of investors.

At least 1,500 people have died in violence which engulfed the country in March and prompted the dispatch of a multinational force helping to keep order for the election. The Balkan country's main political parties signed an accord in Rome on Monday promising to ensure a free and fair vote.
According to government estimates, about $1.2 billion was lost in the collapsed funds. Four other schemes remain in operation but have ceased paying the high interest rates initially promised.

The IMF and World Bank had repeatedly warned Berisha to crack down on the schemes, which offered huge rates of return to investors with little awareness of markets after 45 years of living in eastern Europe's harshest Communist regime.
The proposed legislation was initially approved by parliament but later amended after the IMF and World Bank expressed reservations about its provisions.
It must now be passed by presidential decree as parliament is in recess ahead of the election.
Berisha wants monitoring procedures to extend to the four failed schemes. The Socialists say those schemes must be dealt with by the courts.
The president was forced to call the early election at the height of the March upheaval and to appoint a multi-party government headed by the Socialists.
Berisha's Democrats won a huge majority in last year's general election criticised in Albania and abroad as unfair. This time they face a stiff challenge from the Socialists.
Socialist leader Fatos Nano has told rallies he will try to recover as much of investors' lost money as possible.
"This is to be welcomed," said a Western source in Tirana. "Every effort must be made to recover as much as possible for depositors from funds within and outside Albania."
